CHAPTER XIII.


Their intended excursion to Whitwell turned out very different from
what Elinor had expected. She was prepared to be wet through, fatigued,
and frightened; but the event was still more unfortunate, for they did
not go at all.

By ten o’clock the whole party was assembled at the park, where they
were to breakfast. The morning was rather favourable, though it had
rained all night, as the clouds were then dispersing across the sky,
and the sun frequently appeared. They were all in high spirits and good
humour, eager to be happy, and determined to submit to the greatest
inconveniences and hardships rather than be otherwise.

While they were at breakfast the letters were brought in. Among the
rest there was one for Colonel Brandon;—he took it, looked at the
direction, changed colour, and immediately left the room.

“What is the matter with Brandon?” said Sir John.

Nobody could tell.

“I hope he has had no bad news,” said Lady Middleton. “It must be
something extraordinary that could make Colonel Brandon leave my
breakfast table so suddenly.”

In about five minutes he returned.

“No bad news, Colonel, I hope;” said Mrs. Jennings, as soon as he
entered the room.

“None at all, ma’am, I thank you.”

“Was it from Avignon? I hope it is not to say that your sister is
worse.”

“No, ma’am. It came from town, and is merely a letter of business.”

“But how came the hand to discompose you so much, if it was only a
letter of business? Come, come, this won’t do, Colonel; so let us hear
the truth of it.”

“My dear madam,” said Lady Middleton, “recollect what you are saying.”

“Perhaps it is to tell you that your cousin Fanny is married?” said
Mrs. Jennings, without attending to her daughter’s reproof.

“No, indeed, it is not.”

“Well, then, I know who it is from, Colonel. And I hope she is well.”

“Whom do you mean, ma’am?” said he, colouring a little.

“Oh! you know who I mean.”

“I am particularly sorry, ma’am,” said he, addressing Lady Middleton,
“that I should receive this letter today, for it is on business which
requires my immediate attendance in town.”

“In town!” cried Mrs. Jennings. “What can you have to do in town at
this time of year?”

“My own loss is great,” he continued, “in being obliged to leave so
agreeable a party; but I am the more concerned, as I fear my presence
is necessary to gain your admittance at Whitwell.”

What a blow upon them all was this!

“But if you write a note to the housekeeper, Mr. Brandon,” said
Marianne, eagerly, “will it not be sufficient?”

He shook his head.

“We must go,” said Sir John.—“It shall not be put off when we are so
near it. You cannot go to town till tomorrow, Brandon, that is all.”

“I wish it could be so easily settled. But it is not in my power to
delay my journey for one day!”

“If you would but let us know what your business is,” said Mrs.
Jennings, “we might see whether it could be put off or not.”

“You would not be six hours later,” said Willoughby, “if you were to
defer your journey till our return.”

“I cannot afford to lose _one_ hour.”

Elinor then heard Willoughby say, in a low voice to Marianne, “There
are some people who cannot bear a party of pleasure. Brandon is one of
them. He was afraid of catching cold I dare say, and invented this
trick for getting out of it. I would lay fifty guineas the letter was
of his own writing.”

“I have no doubt of it,” replied Marianne.

“There is no persuading you to change your mind, Brandon, I know of
old,” said Sir John, “when once you are determined on anything. But,
however, I hope you will think better of it. Consider, here are the two
Miss Careys come over from Newton, the three Miss Dashwoods walked up
from the cottage, and Mr. Willoughby got up two hours before his usual
time, on purpose to go to Whitwell.”

Colonel Brandon again repeated his sorrow at being the cause of
disappointing the party; but at the same time declared it to be
unavoidable.

“Well, then, when will you come back again?”

“I hope we shall see you at Barton,” added her ladyship, “as soon as
you can conveniently leave town; and we must put off the party to
Whitwell till you return.”

“You are very obliging. But it is so uncertain, when I may have it in
my power to return, that I dare not engage for it at all.”

“Oh! he must and shall come back,” cried Sir John. “If he is not here
by the end of the week, I shall go after him.”

“Ay, so do, Sir John,” cried Mrs. Jennings, “and then perhaps you may
find out what his business is.”

“I do not want to pry into other men’s concerns. I suppose it is
something he is ashamed of.”

Colonel Brandon’s horses were announced.

“You do not go to town on horseback, do you?” added Sir John.

“No. Only to Honiton. I shall then go post.”

“Well, as you are resolved to go, I wish you a good journey. But you
had better change your mind.”

“I assure you it is not in my power.”

He then took leave of the whole party.

“Is there no chance of my seeing you and your sisters in town this
winter, Miss Dashwood?”

“I am afraid, none at all.”

“Then I must bid you farewell for a longer time than I should wish to
do.”

To Marianne, he merely bowed and said nothing.

“Come Colonel,” said Mrs. Jennings, “before you go, do let us know what
you are going about.”

He wished her a good morning, and, attended by Sir John, left the room.

The complaints and lamentations which politeness had hitherto
restrained, now burst forth universally; and they all agreed again and
again how provoking it was to be so disappointed.

“I can guess what his business is, however,” said Mrs. Jennings
exultingly.

“Can you, ma’am?” said almost every body.

“Yes; it is about Miss Williams, I am sure.”

“And who is Miss Williams?” asked Marianne.

“What! do not you know who Miss Williams is? I am sure you must have
heard of her before. She is a relation of the Colonel’s, my dear; a
very near relation. We will not say how near, for fear of shocking the
young ladies.” Then, lowering her voice a little, she said to Elinor,
“She is his natural daughter.”

“Indeed!”

“Oh, yes; and as like him as she can stare. I dare say the Colonel will
leave her all his fortune.”

When Sir John returned, he joined most heartily in the general regret
on so unfortunate an event; concluding however by observing, that as
they were all got together, they must do something by way of being
happy; and after some consultation it was agreed, that although
happiness could only be enjoyed at Whitwell, they might procure a
tolerable composure of mind by driving about the country. The carriages
were then ordered; Willoughby’s was first, and Marianne never looked
happier than when she got into it. He drove through the park very fast,
and they were soon out of sight; and nothing more of them was seen till
their return, which did not happen till after the return of all the
rest. They both seemed delighted with their drive; but said only in
general terms that they had kept in the lanes, while the others went on
the downs.

It was settled that there should be a dance in the evening, and that
every body should be extremely merry all day long. Some more of the
Careys came to dinner, and they had the pleasure of sitting down nearly
twenty to table, which Sir John observed with great contentment.
Willoughby took his usual place between the two elder Miss Dashwoods.
Mrs. Jennings sat on Elinor’s right hand; and they had not been long
seated, before she leant behind her and Willoughby, and said to
Marianne, loud enough for them both to hear, “I have found you out in
spite of all your tricks. I know where you spent the morning.”

Marianne coloured, and replied very hastily, “Where, pray?”

“Did not you know,” said Willoughby, “that we had been out in my
curricle?”

“Yes, yes, Mr. Impudence, I know that very well, and I was determined
to find out _where_ you had been to. I hope you like your house, Miss
Marianne. It is a very large one, I know; and when I come to see you, I
hope you will have new-furnished it, for it wanted it very much when I
was there six years ago.”

Marianne turned away in great confusion. Mrs. Jennings laughed
heartily; and Elinor found that in her resolution to know where they
had been, she had actually made her own woman enquire of Mr.
Willoughby’s groom; and that she had by that method been informed that
they had gone to Allenham, and spent a considerable time there in
walking about the garden and going all over the house.

Elinor could hardly believe this to be true, as it seemed very unlikely
that Willoughby should propose, or Marianne consent, to enter the house
while Mrs. Smith was in it, with whom Marianne had not the smallest
acquaintance.

As soon as they left the dining-room, Elinor enquired of her about it;
and great was her surprise when she found that every circumstance
related by Mrs. Jennings was perfectly true. Marianne was quite angry
with her for doubting it.

“Why should you imagine, Elinor, that we did not go there, or that we
did not see the house? Is not it what you have often wished to do
yourself?”

“Yes, Marianne, but I would not go while Mrs. Smith was there, and with
no other companion than Mr. Willoughby.”

“Mr. Willoughby however is the only person who can have a right to show
that house; and as he went in an open carriage, it was impossible to
have any other companion. I never spent a pleasanter morning in my
life.”

“I am afraid,” replied Elinor, “that the pleasantness of an employment
does not always evince its propriety.”

“On the contrary, nothing can be a stronger proof of it, Elinor; for if
there had been any real impropriety in what I did, I should have been
sensible of it at the time, for we always know when we are acting
wrong, and with such a conviction I could have had no pleasure.”

“But, my dear Marianne, as it has already exposed you to some very
impertinent remarks, do you not now begin to doubt the discretion of
your own conduct?”

“If the impertinent remarks of Mrs. Jennings are to be the proof of
impropriety in conduct, we are all offending every moment of our lives.
I value not her censure any more than I should do her commendation. I
am not sensible of having done anything wrong in walking over Mrs.
Smith’s grounds, or in seeing her house. They will one day be Mr.
Willoughby’s, and—”

“If they were one day to be your own, Marianne, you would not be
justified in what you have done.”

She blushed at this hint; but it was even visibly gratifying to her;
and after a ten minutes’ interval of earnest thought, she came to her
sister again, and said with great good humour, “Perhaps, Elinor, it
_was_ rather ill-judged in me to go to Allenham; but Mr. Willoughby
wanted particularly to show me the place; and it is a charming house, I
assure you.—There is one remarkably pretty sitting room up stairs; of a
nice comfortable size for constant use, and with modern furniture it
would be delightful. It is a corner room, and has windows on two sides.
On one side you look across the bowling-green, behind the house, to a
beautiful hanging wood, and on the other you have a view of the church
and village, and, beyond them, of those fine bold hills that we have so
often admired. I did not see it to advantage, for nothing could be more
forlorn than the furniture,—but if it were newly fitted up—a couple of
hundred pounds, Willoughby says, would make it one of the pleasantest
summer-rooms in England.”

Could Elinor have listened to her without interruption from the others,
she would have described every room in the house with equal delight.

Elinor had braced herself for their planned Whitwell excursion for days: she’d stowed a spare wool shawl and change of stockings in her bag, fully expecting to return soaked through, footsore, and giddy from a day out on the wild rolling countryside. What she never anticipated was that they would not leave Barton Park at all.

By ten o’clock that morning, the whole merry party had assembled for breakfast at the Park. The previous night’s heavy rain had all but blown itself out; clouds drifted thin across pale blue sky, and bursts of golden sunlight broke through every few minutes to gild the wet lawns. Spirits ran high. Everyone chattered over buttered crumpets and spiced cider, all agreeing they would endure any mud, any chill, any inconvenience to make the day perfect.

Then the post was brought in. One letter, addressed in a sharp unfamiliar hand, landed beside Colonel Brandon. He picked it up, glanced at the seal, and the colour drained from his face entirely. Without a word, he pushed back his chair and left the breakfast parlour in such a hurry the door swung shut behind him with a soft bang.
“Now what’s got into Brandon?” Sir John exclaimed, tapping his knife against the edge of his plate. No one could guess. “I do hope no harm has befallen anyone,” Lady Middleton said smoothly, lifting her teacup. “It must be a very extraordinary matter to pull Colonel Brandon away from my breakfast table so abruptly.”

Five minutes later, he returned, his jaw tight, his usual gentle smile forced.
“No bad news, I hope, Colonel?” Mrs. Jennings called out the second he crossed the threshold.
“None at all, ma’am, I thank you.”
“Was it from Avignon? I do hope your sister’s health hasn’t worsened?”
“No, ma’am. It came from London, only a letter of business.”
“Business, my foot,” Mrs. Jennings hooted, leaning forward. “A plain business letter wouldn’t make you turn that pale. Come now, Colonel, no secrets from old friends.”
“Mamma, do mind your manners,” Lady Middleton chided.
“Maybe it’s news your cousin Fanny’s finally married off?” Mrs. Jennings went on, ignoring her daughter entirely.
“Indeed it is not.”
“Well then, I know exactly who wrote it,” she grinned, winking. “I hope the dear girl is quite well?”
Colonel Brandon flushed faintly. “Who do you mean, ma’am?”
“Oh, you know perfectly well.” He turned to Lady Middleton, his tone rueful. “I am very sorry to say this, but the business in that letter demands I leave for London at once. I cannot delay a single day.”

“London?” Mrs. Jennings squawked. “What on earth could possibly need you in town in the middle of the country summer?”
“It grieves me greatly to leave such a pleasant gathering,” he went on, “but what is worse, I fear my personal presence is required to secure our admittance to Whitwell. The steward will not unlock the grounds for anyone else.”

A collective groan rippled across the table. Marianne leaned forward at once, eyes bright and eager. “If you write a note directly to the housekeeper, would that not be enough?”
He shook his head.
“Then we shall still go!” Sir John boomed, slamming his fist lightly on the table. “We are almost there already, no need to call the whole thing off. You can leave for London tomorrow, Brandon, no harm done.”
“I wish it were that easy. I have not a single hour to spare.”
Willoughby leaned back in his chair, amused. “If you would only delay your journey six hours, wait for us to return from Whitwell, you would not be behind at all.”
“I cannot.”

Elinor caught the low murmur Willoughby whispered directly in Marianne’s ear, his tone teasing: “Some folks simply cannot bear a day of unplanned fun. I’d wager fifty guineas that letter he received was written in his own hand, just to get out of the trip.”
Marianne’s eyes crinkled with a secret smile as she whispered back, “I have no doubt of it at all.”

Sir John spent another ten minutes arguing with him to change his mind, listing off all the people who had traveled specially for the excursion: the two Miss Careys from Newton, the three Miss Dashwoods walking all the way up from the cottage, Willoughby rising two hours earlier than usual just to make the dawn start. But Colonel Brandon would not budge.
“Then when will you be back?” Lady Middleton asked, softening. “We shall just reschedule the Whitwell trip for when you return, of course.”
“You are very kind. But I cannot possibly say when my business will allow me to come back. I cannot promise a date at all.”
“Oh, he’ll be back by the end of the week, or I shall ride to London and drag him home myself!” Sir John laughed.
“Quite right,” Mrs. Jennings cackled. “Then we might finally find out what this mysterious business of his is.”
“I do not pry into other men’s secrets,” Sir John said, “but I half suspect it is something he is too embarrassed to admit to.”

Colonel Brandon’s horses were announced at that moment. “You are not riding all the way to London, are you?” Sir John asked, surprised.
“Only as far as Honiton. I shall take a post-chaise from there. I truly cannot delay.”
He went around the table to take his leave of everyone. When he reached Elinor, he paused. “I hope I shall have the chance to see you and your sisters in London this winter?”
“I am afraid that is very unlikely,” Elinor said gently.
“Then I must say goodbye for far longer than I would wish.” To Marianne, he gave only a quiet, reserved bow, no words at all, before he followed Sir John out of the room.

No sooner had the door shut than all the polite restraint vanished. Everyone complained at once, bemoaning how cruel it was to have their perfect day spoiled.
“But I know exactly what his secret business is!” Mrs. Jennings announced, triumphant.
“Who is it, ma’am?” half the table chorused.
“Miss Williams, of course! She is a very near relation of the Colonel’s—so near I daren’t say exactly how, for fear of shocking you young ladies,” she lowered her voice to Elinor’s ear. “His natural daughter, my dear. The spitting image of him, too. Mark my words, he will leave her every penny he owns.”

When Sir John trundled back into the parlour a few minutes later, he threw his support behind a new plan: they would not waste the rest of the day. Since Whitwell was out of reach, they would take carriages and drive all across the surrounding countryside, make their own fun.
The first carriage brought round was Willoughby’s bright, flashy curricle. Marianne did not hesitate a second before hopping up onto the seat beside him, her face lit up brighter than the sun. He snapped the reins, and the pair tore off down the park drive at a gallop, vanishing down the lanes long before the rest of the party had even climbed into their own carriages. They were gone for hours, only returning long after everyone else had finished their slow drive across the downs. Both were pink-cheeked, glowing, and refused to say anything more than that they had stuck to the quiet little back lanes, far away from other travelers.

That evening, a dance was planned, and more guests arrived for dinner, until nearly twenty people sat around the long table. Willoughby took his usual place between Elinor and Marianne, while Mrs. Jennings sat on Elinor’s right. They had barely begun their first course before Mrs. Jennings leaned across the back of Elinor’s chair, her voice loud enough for both Marianne and Willoughby to hear, cackling. “I found you two out, no matter how you tried to hide it. I know exactly where you spent your morning.”
Marianne blushed scarlet. “Wherever do you mean?”
“Did you think I would not notice you took the curricle out?” Willoughby laughed.
“Oh, I knew that, you impudent thing,” Mrs. Jennings said, grinning. “I sent my maid to ask your groom, and he told me every last detail. You drove out to Allenham, did you not? Spent hours wandering the gardens and walking all through the great house? I do hope you liked it, Miss Marianne. It is a lovely big place, though it was dreadfully in need of new furniture when I visited six years ago. When I come to call on you there someday, I do hope you will have fitted it all out new.”

Marianne turned away, flustered beyond words, while Mrs. Jennings laughed so hard her wig tilted sideways. Elinor could scarcely believe it. It seemed utterly improper that Willoughby would bring Marianne to Allenham, to wander through Mrs. Smith’s private home, when Marianne had never even been introduced to the old lady. No sooner had they left the dining parlour than she pulled Marianne aside to question her. She was even more shocked to find every word Mrs. Jennings had said was entirely true.
“Why on earth would you think we should not go?” Marianne said, half cross that Elinor would doubt her. “You have said a hundred times you wished to see the inside of Allenham yourself.”
“I did, but I would never go traipsing through it while the owner was inside, with no chaperone but Mr. Willoughby!”
“Willoughby is the only person who has a right to show that house off. And we were in an open curricle, there was no room for any other guest. I never had a happier morning in all my life.”
“Just because it was pleasant does not mean it was proper, Marianne.”
“Nonsense! If there had been anything wrong with what we did, I would have felt it at once. You always know when you are acting incorrectly, and I could never have been that happy if I had done something wrong.”
“But the gossip from Mrs. Jennings—does that not make you wonder if you were a little unwise?”
“If every silly remark Mrs. Jennings makes counts as proof of impropriety, we would all be sinning every minute of the day. I care no more for her censure than I do for her praise. We only walked through the grounds and the empty rooms of the house. It will be Willoughby’s home one day, after all—”
“Even if it was to be your home one day, Marianne, that does not make it right to wander through it uninvited now.”

Marianne blushed deep, but her smile was so bright, so full of quiet delight, that Elinor did not have the heart to scold her further. After ten minutes of quiet, dreamy thought, Marianne came back to Elinor, gushing, “It really was so lovely, Elinor. There is that little corner sitting room upstairs, you know? Windows on two whole sides. One looks over the bowling green, past the hanging woods down to the valley, the other looks straight out at the church, the village, and all those steep, wild hills we love so much. The furniture is terribly shabby right now, but Willoughby says a mere two hundred pounds would turn it into the nicest summer parlour in all of England.”
If the rest of the party had not been chattering and calling them over to the dancing room, Marianne would have happily described every single room in the great house, down to the smallest cupboard, and Elinor would have sat and listened, knowing full well her sister was already mapping out the rest of her life there, hand in hand with Willoughby.
